To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we propose a simple but powerful few-shot classification method for domain-agnostic few-shot classification.

1) we propose to train a single model for few-shot classification that is agnostic to the underlying domain distribution; 2) we propose a new method that learns a domain-specific modulator for each task and uses it to adapt the model for the new task; 3) we show that this method outperforms existing state-of-the-art few-shot classification methods on several datasets.

(i) we propose a novel few-shot learning method that is domain-agnostic, (ii) we show that the proposed method can generalize to unseen domains, and (iii) the proposed method is easy to implement and is competitive with state-of-the-art methods
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: How to learn a model that generalizes to unseen domains? How to learn a few-shot classifier from a task distribution that spans multiple domains?
how to learn a few-shot classification model that is robust to domain shifts.

our method is a simple but effective approach to few-shot classification, which is domain agnostic.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we propose a novel meta-learning framework for few-shot classification that can learn domain-agnostic modulators to adaptively modulate the feature extractor and the task-specific classifier for each task.
we introduce a novel few-shot classification model that can learn to adapt to unseen domains.
we learn to modulate the feature extractor and the classifier in a way that they are domain-aware.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the meta-learning framework is not limited to learning a model that can generalize across a single domain, but can also learn a model that can handle a variety of domains.
we learn a single modulator for all domains by using domain-agnostic meta-training examples and then use the modulator for few-shot classification on a target domain.
a single meta-model trained on multiple domains is more effective than the one trained on a single domain.
